nameStory: The Green-legged Orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive greenish coloration on its legs, which sets it apart from many of its brown and gray relatives. This vibrant leg color makes it one of the more easily recognizable members of the orbweaver family. The scientific name 'maculata' means 'spotted,' referring to the markings on its abdomen.
description: The Green-legged Orbweaver is a small to medium-sized spider that builds the classic circular webs we often associate with spiders. True to its name, this orbweaver sports greenish legs that contrast beautifully with its typically brownish or grayish body. Like other orbweavers, it has a rounded abdomen and relatively compact build. These spiders are part of the large orbweaver family, known for their geometric web-spinning abilities.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive greenish coloration on the legs, which may appear yellowish-green to pale green depending on lighting and the spider's age

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds typical orb webs - circular, symmetrical webs with radiating spokes and spiral capture threads that feel sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with a relatively small cephalothorax (front body section), giving it a somewhat egg-shaped profile when viewed from above

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small to medium orbweaver, with females noticeably larger than males, though still easily fitting on a quarter coin

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web during evening hours, but may hide in nearby foliage during the day with a signal thread connecting to the web

habitat: Green-legged Orbweavers favor gardens, woodland edges, and areas with mixed vegetation where they can anchor their webs between shrubs, tall grasses, or low tree branches. They particularly like spots with some morning sun but afternoon shade, often building webs 2-4 feet off the ground. Look for them in areas where flying insects are common, such as near flowering plants or garden borders.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring, starting to build their first webs of the season as insect prey becomes more abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen. This is the best time to spot their distinctive green legs and observe their web-building behavior.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced. Adults may still be active into early fall before dying off with the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as eggs in protected locations. No adult spiders are active during the cold months.

funFact: Green-legged Orbweavers can actually tune the tension of their web threads like guitar strings, adjusting the vibration frequency to better detect different types of prey struggling in their webs!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small orbweavers, but the greenish leg coloration is usually distinctive enough to set it apart. Remember: 'Green legs, easy ID' - if you see those pale green or yellowish-green legs on a small orbweaver, you've likely found your spider.
compareHints: Among its Mangora relatives, the Green-legged Orbweaver is distinguished by its leg coloration - the Tuft-legged Orbweaver has hair tufts on its legs instead of green coloring, while the Lined Orbweaver shows distinct linear markings on its abdomen. The green legs are really the key feature that separates this species from its close cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Mangora relatives, the Tuft-legged Orbweaver is distinguished by having the most prominent leg tufts and more subdued coloring.

Among its Mangora relatives, the lined orbweaver's striped pattern is more pronounced than the tuft-legged orbweaver's subtle markings, and lacks the distinctive green coloration of the green-legged orbweaver.
